1.name: Tropical & Subtropical Moist Broadleaf Forests
1.about: Closed-canopy forest with year-round warmth and heavy rain. The most species-rich habitat on land: half of all described species live in rainforest covering about 7% of the planet.

2.name: Tropical & Subtropical Dry Broadleaf Forests
2.about: Warm all year with a long, severe dry season. Most trees drop their leaves to survive it, so the forest floor swings between deep shade and open sunlight.

3.name: Tropical & Subtropical Coniferous Forests
3.about: Pine and other conifers at low latitudes, usually on poor soils, ridgelines or fire-swept slopes where broadleaf trees cannot hold on.

4.name: Temperate Broadleaf & Mixed Forests
4.about: Four distinct seasons and deciduous trees that shed leaves before winter. Heavily settled by people — much of the original extent is farmland or regrowth.

5.name: Temperate Conifer Forests
5.about: Evergreen needle-leaf forest in mild, wet or mountainous temperate zones. Includes the tallest and most massive trees alive.

6.name: Boreal Forests/Taiga
6.about: The largest continuous forest on Earth, ringing the northern hemisphere. Short cool summers, brutal winters, and only a handful of tree species.

7.name: Tropical & Subtropical Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands
7.about: Grass-dominated country with scattered trees, shaped by seasonal rain, fire and large grazing animals. Home to the planet's biggest surviving herds.

8.name: Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands
8.about: Prairie, steppe and pampas. Too dry for forest, too wet for desert — deep soils that made these the world's most thoroughly ploughed biome.

9.name: Flooded Grasslands & Savannas
9.about: Grassland that floods on a seasonal or permanent cycle. Small in area but extraordinary for waterbirds, which gather here in enormous concentrations.

10.name: Montane Grasslands & Shrublands
10.about: High-elevation grass and scrub above the treeline. Intense sun, thin air and freezing nights select for compact, hairy, slow-growing plants.

11.name: Tundra
11.about: Treeless ground underlain by permafrost. The growing season is measured in weeks, and almost all plant mass sits below the surface.

12.name: Mediterranean Forests, Woodlands & Scrub
12.about: Hot dry summers, mild wet winters. Only five small patches worldwide, and all five are exceptionally rich in plants found nowhere else.

13.name: Deserts & Xeric Shrublands
13.about: Less than 250 mm of rain a year, or evaporation that far outstrips it. Life here is built around storing water and avoiding heat.

14.name: Mangroves
14.about: Salt-tolerant forest along tropical coasts, rooted in tidal mud. Acts as nursery for reef fish and as the coast's first defence against storms.

AF.name: Afrotropic
AF.about: Sub-Saharan Africa, Madagascar and southern Arabia. The one realm that kept its full megafauna through the Pleistocene extinctions.

AN.name: Antarctica
AN.about: The southern polar continent. Terrestrial life is reduced to two flowering plants, mosses, lichens and invertebrates.

AU.name: Australasia
AU.about: Australia, New Guinea, New Zealand and eastern Indonesia beyond Wallace's Line. Marsupials and ancient Gondwanan lineages dominate.

IN.name: Indomalayan
IN.about: South and Southeast Asia from Pakistan to Wallacea. Dense human population layered over some of the richest forests on Earth.

NE.name: Nearctic
NE.about: North America down to the Mexican highlands. Shares deep history with the Palearctic across the old Bering land bridge.

NO.name: Neotropic
NO.about: South and Central America and the Caribbean. Isolated for tens of millions of years — the most species-rich realm of all.

OC.name: Oceania
OC.about: Remote Pacific islands. Tiny land area, extreme endemism, and the highest extinction rate of any realm.

PA.name: Palearctic
PA.about: Europe, North Africa, and Asia north of the Himalaya. Vast, cold-adapted, and the longest continuously settled by humans.

AF01.title: Congo Basin & Guinean rainforest
AF01.about: The second largest rainforest on Earth. Lowland Congolian forest holds intact elephant and great-ape populations; the West African Guinean block is far more fragmented.

AF02.title: Madagascar & Zambezian dry forest
AF02.about: Madagascar's western dry deciduous forest is one of the most threatened forest types anywhere — reduced to fragments, yet almost everything in it is endemic.

AF07.title: African savanna & miombo woodland
AF07.about: The classic African savanna belt — Sahel, Sudanian, Serengeti and the miombo woodlands. Still carries the largest intact assemblage of big mammals on Earth.

AF08.title: South Atlantic island grassland
AF08.about: Tristan da Cunha, Gough and Amsterdam Island — tiny, wind-hammered specks of temperate grassland that serve as globally critical seabird colonies.

AF09.title: African flooded grassland
AF09.about: The Sudd, Okavango, Bangweulu and Lake Chad — inland deltas and seasonal floodplains that concentrate staggering numbers of waterbirds and antelope.

AF10.title: Ethiopian & African montane grassland
AF10.about: Sky islands — the Ethiopian Highlands, Drakensberg and Albertine Rift peaks. Long isolation above the surrounding lowlands has produced dense endemism.

AF12.title: Cape fynbos & Albany thicket
AF12.about: The Cape Floristic Region: the smallest of the world's six floral kingdoms, and by some measures the richest flora on Earth for its area. Fire is essential to it.

AF13.title: Namib, Kalahari & Karoo
AF13.about: From the Namib — the oldest desert on Earth, watered mainly by coastal fog — to the Karoo's succulent shrublands and the Kalahari's sand sheets.

AF14.title: African mangroves
AF14.about: Mangrove belts along the Guinean and Central African coasts, East Africa and Madagascar — nurseries for coastal fisheries and buffers against erosion.

AN11.title: Antarctic tundra
AN11.about: Ice-free rock and the Antarctic Peninsula. Just two native flowering plants exist on the whole continent; the food web runs on the sea, not the land.

AU01.title: New Guinea & Moluccan rainforest
AU01.about: New Guinea holds perhaps 5% of the world's species on under 1% of its land, and remains one of the least biologically explored places on Earth.

variants.title: Sulawesi & Wallacean rainforest
variants.about: Islands between Asia and Australia that were never joined to either. Sulawesi's fauna is unlike anything on the continents on either side.

AU02.title: Lesser Sunda & New Caledonia dry forest
AU02.about: Monsoon-dry islands east of Bali plus New Caledonia's dry forest — the latter reduced to about 1% of its original extent.

AU04.title: Australian & New Zealand temperate forest
AU04.about: Eucalypt forest along Australia's southeast plus New Zealand's podocarp and kauri forest — the latter evolved with no land mammals at all, so birds took every role.

AU07.title: Northern Australian savanna
AU07.about: The tropical north — Kimberley, Arnhem Land and the Gulf country. One of the largest savannas left largely intact, though fire regimes and cane toads have reshaped it.

AU08.title: Australian & NZ temperate grassland
AU08.about: Mulga shrubland, southeastern temperate savanna and New Zealand's tussock grasslands — heavily grazed, and among Australia's most-cleared vegetation types.

AU10.title: Australasian alpine grassland
AU10.about: The Australian Alps, New Zealand's Southern Alps and New Guinea's high central range — small, cold islands above the treeline.

AU11.title: Subantarctic island tundra
AU11.about: The Antipodes and neighbouring subantarctic islands — cold, wet, wind-scoured, and disproportionately important as seabird breeding grounds.

AU12.title: Southwest Australian mallee & woodland
AU12.about: Mallee eucalypts and the Southwest Australian Floristic Region — a global biodiversity hotspot with thousands of plants found nowhere else.

AU13.title: Australian deserts
AU13.about: The Great Sandy, Simpson, Gibson and Great Victoria deserts — the red centre. Rainfall is erratic rather than merely scarce, so life runs in boom and bust.

AU14.title: New Guinea mangroves
AU14.about: Extensive, largely intact mangrove along New Guinea's southern and northern coasts — among the least disturbed mangrove systems left.

IN01.title: Indomalayan rainforest
IN01.about: Sundaland, Indochina and the Western Ghats. Borneo and Sumatra alone hold species found on no other island, and are losing forest faster than almost anywhere.

variants.title: Western Ghats & Sri Lanka rainforest
variants.about: A narrow wet strip along India's west coast plus Sri Lanka's hills — older than the Himalaya and one of the world's densest concentrations of endemic amphibians.

IN02.title: Indian & Indochinese dry forest
IN02.about: Teak and sal dry deciduous forest across central India and Indochina. Gir Forest is the last wild refuge of the Asiatic lion.

IN03.title: Tropical Asian pine forest
IN03.about: Pine on Himalayan foothills, the Luzon highlands and Sumatra's ridges — fire-adapted conifer forest deep inside the tropics.

IN04.title: Himalayan broadleaf forest
IN04.about: Mid-elevation oak, laurel and rhododendron forest on the Himalayan front — a steep gradient that packs many life zones into a short vertical distance.

IN05.title: Himalayan subalpine conifer forest
IN05.about: Fir, spruce and birch just below the treeline, giving way to rhododendron scrub — the last forest before the alpine zone.

IN07.title: Terai-Duar savanna
IN07.about: A narrow belt of tall elephant grass and riverine forest along the Himalayan foot. Some of the tallest grassland on Earth, and prime tiger and rhino habitat.

IN09.title: Rann of Kutch salt marsh
IN09.about: A vast seasonal salt flat that floods with the monsoon then bakes dry — the only home of the Indian wild ass and a major flamingo breeding site.

IN10.title: Kinabalu alpine meadow
IN10.about: A single tiny alpine zone atop Mount Kinabalu in Borneo — an isolated cold island surrounded by tropical rainforest, packed with endemics.

IN13.title: Thar Desert & Deccan thorn scrub
IN13.about: The Thar is the most densely populated desert on Earth. Thorn scrub across the Deccan and Indus valley completes the realm's dry end.

IN14.title: Sundarbans & Southeast Asian mangroves
IN14.about: The Sundarbans is the largest mangrove forest in the world and the only mangrove anywhere with a resident tiger population.

NE02.title: Sonoran-Sinaloan dry forest
NE02.about: Thornscrub and dry forest on Mexico's northwest coast — a transition between the Sonoran Desert and true tropical forest.

NE03.title: Sierra Madre pine-oak forest
NE03.about: The Sierra Madre Occidental and Oriental hold the world's greatest diversity of pines and oaks, and the wintering grounds of the monarch butterfly nearby.

NE04.title: Eastern North American forest
NE04.about: Appalachian and Great Lakes hardwood forest. The southern Appalachians hold the richest salamander fauna on Earth.

NE05.title: Western North American conifer forest
NE05.about: Rockies, Cascades and the Pacific coast. The coastal strip grows the tallest trees on Earth and the largest by volume.

NE06.title: North American boreal forest
NE06.about: Canada's boreal shield and Alaskan taiga — the nursery for billions of North America's migratory songbirds each summer.

NE07.title: Western Gulf coastal grassland
NE07.about: Coastal prairie along the Gulf of Mexico — over 99% converted to farmland and ranch, and the wintering range of the whooping crane.

NE08.title: Great Plains prairie
NE08.about: Tallgrass, mixed and shortgrass prairie. Once carried tens of millions of bison; now among the most completely converted ecosystems on the continent.

NE11.title: Arctic North American tundra
NE11.about: Canadian and Greenlandic Arctic tundra. Permafrost holds enormous carbon stocks, and the surface thaws only a few weeks each year.

NE12.title: California chaparral
NE12.about: California's Mediterranean scrub and oak woodland — one of only five such regions worldwide, and a biodiversity hotspot shaped by fire.

NE13.title: North American deserts
NE13.about: Sonoran, Chihuahuan, Mojave and Great Basin. The Sonoran is the wettest and most vegetated hot desert in the world; the Great Basin is cold and sagebrush-dominated.

OC01.title: Pacific island rainforest
OC01.about: Hawai'i, Fiji, Samoa and Micronesia. Extreme isolation drove spectacular radiations — and made these the most extinction-prone ecosystems on Earth.

NO01.title: Amazon & Atlantic rainforest
NO01.about: The Amazon is the largest rainforest on Earth; Brazil's Atlantic Forest is separately one of the most endemic-rich and most reduced, at roughly 12% of its original extent.

variants.title: Atlantic Forest
variants.about: Brazil's coastal rainforest, now reduced to roughly a tenth of its original extent — and still one of the most endemic-rich forests on Earth.

NO02.title: Neotropical dry forest & Caatinga
NO02.about: The Caatinga, Chiquitano and Chaco-edge dry forests. Caatinga is the largest dry forest in South America and exists nowhere else.

variants.title: Mesoamerican dry forest
variants.about: Seasonally dry forest down Mexico's Pacific slope and into Central America — extremely rich in endemics and far more threatened than the region's rainforest.

NO03.title: Mesoamerican & Caribbean pine forest
NO03.about: Highland pine-oak from Mexico through Honduras, plus Caribbean pineyards. Cloud-forest patches within it hold the resplendent quetzal.

NO04.title: Valdivian & Magellanic temperate forest
NO04.about: South America's temperate rainforest — a Gondwanan relic isolated by the Andes, the Pacific and the Atacama, with strong links to New Zealand's flora.

NO07.title: Cerrado, Llanos & Chaco
NO07.about: The Cerrado is the most species-rich savanna on Earth and a fast-disappearing one; the Llanos and Chaco complete South America's dry grassland belt.

NO08.title: Pampas & Patagonian steppe
NO08.about: The humid Pampas grassland and, in the Andes' rain shadow, the cold windswept Patagonian steppe.

NO09.title: Pantanal, Everglades & Orinoco wetlands
NO09.about: The Pantanal is the largest tropical wetland on Earth and the best place anywhere to see wild jaguar; the Everglades is a slow, shallow river of grass.

NO10.title: Andean páramo & puna
NO10.about: High Andean grassland from the wet páramo of the north to the dry puna of Bolivia and Chile — much of it above 4,000 m, and a centre of crop domestication.

NO12.title: Chilean matorral
NO12.about: Chile's Mediterranean scrub, hemmed in by the Andes, the Atacama and the Pacific. Small, densely populated, and highly endemic.

NO13.title: Atacama, Sechura & Galápagos scrub
NO13.about: The Atacama is the driest non-polar desert on Earth — some weather stations have never recorded rain. The Galápagos scrub sits in the same cold-current rain shadow.

NO14.title: Neotropical mangroves
NO14.about: Caribbean, Amazon-delta and Pacific-coast mangrove — the Amazon-Orinoco belt is one of the largest continuous mangrove systems in the world.

PA01.title: South China subtropical forest
PA01.about: Yunnan and Guizhou plateau evergreen broadleaf forest — a warm, wet corner of the Palearctic that grades into the Indomalayan realm.

PA04.title: European temperate forest
PA04.about: Broadleaf and mixed forest across Europe, worked by people for millennia — very little is primary, and Białowieża on the Polish-Belarusian border is the best-preserved remnant.

variants.title: Manchurian & Far Eastern forest
variants.about: Mixed forest of Manchuria, Korea, Japan and the Russian Far East — the last stronghold of the Amur tiger and Amur leopard.

PA05.title: Alpine & Siberian montane conifer forest
PA05.about: Conifer forest of the Alps, Carpathians, Altai and Sayan — spruce, fir, larch and stone pine on slopes too steep or cold for broadleaf trees.

variants.title: Hengduan Mountains conifer forest
variants.about: Southwest China's north-south mountain chains — one of the richest temperate floras on Earth, and the wild range of the giant panda.

PA06.title: Siberian & Scandinavian taiga
PA06.about: The largest forest on the planet, stretching from Norway to the Pacific. Underlain by permafrost across much of Siberia and warming faster than the global average.

PA08.title: Pontic & Kazakh steppe
PA08.about: The western half of the Eurasian grass corridor, from the Hungarian puszta to Kazakhstan. Deep black soils made it some of the most completely ploughed land on Earth.

variants.title: Mongolian-Manchurian grassland
variants.about: The eastern steppe. Mongolia's grasslands still carry one of the last great ungulate migrations left in Eurasia.

PA09.title: Amur & East Asian wet meadow
PA09.about: Meadow steppe and floodplain along the Amur and Khanka basins — critical breeding and staging ground on the East Asian flyway.

variants.title: Mesopotamian & Nile wetlands
variants.about: The Tigris-Euphrates marshes and the Nile Delta — ancient wetlands, drained and re-flooded, still vital to migratory birds.

PA10.title: Tibetan Plateau & Central Asian alpine
PA10.about: The Tibetan Plateau — the 'third pole' — plus the Tian Shan and Pamir. Averaging over 4,500 m, it drives the Asian monsoon and feeds Asia's great rivers.

PA11.title: Siberian Arctic tundra
PA11.about: Russian Arctic tundra from Yamal to Chukotka — vast, roadless, and sitting on some of the most carbon-rich permafrost on Earth.

PA12.title: Mediterranean Basin
PA12.about: Olive, oak and maquis around the Mediterranean — a biodiversity hotspot shaped by 8,000 years of farming, grazing and fire.

PA13.title: Sahara & Arabian desert
PA13.about: The largest hot desert on Earth plus the Arabian sand seas. Rainfall is negligible and the daily temperature swing is among the widest anywhere.

variants.title: Gobi, Taklimakan & Central Asian desert
variants.about: Cold continental desert deep inside Asia — the Gobi, Taklimakan, Karakum and Kyzylkum, thousands of kilometres from any ocean.

Tropical coral sea.about: Warm, clear, nutrient-poor shelf water where reef-building corals thrive. Coral reefs cover under 0.1% of the ocean floor yet support roughly a quarter of all marine species.

Warm-temperate shelf.about: Subtropical to warm-temperate continental shelf. Too cool for extensive reefs, too warm for kelp forest — a mix of seagrass, rocky reef and soft sediment.

Cold-temperate shelf.about: Cool, productive shelf seas. Kelp forests, rich fishing grounds, and the seasonal plankton blooms that drive them.

Polar shelf & sea ice.about: Shelf water at or below freezing, covered by ice for much of the year. Life is timed to the brief burst of light when the ice retreats.

Subtropical gyre.about: The great rotating deserts of the open ocean. Nutrient-starved, strikingly clear and blue, and among the least productive water on Earth.

Equatorial current.about: Where divergent currents draw deep water to the surface along the equator, feeding a narrow band of high productivity across an ocean basin.

Western boundary current.about: Fast, warm, deep western-edge currents — the Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Agulhas. They carry tropical heat and tropical animals far towards the poles.

Eastern boundary upwelling.about: Cold nutrient-rich water dragged up along continental west coasts. Under 1% of ocean area, but a fifth of the world's fish catch.

Semi-enclosed sea.about: Seas nearly ringed by land — the Mediterranean, Red Sea, Black Sea. Restricted exchange makes them warm, salty or stratified, and often highly endemic.

Transitional open ocean.about: Where subtropical and subpolar water meet. Sharp temperature fronts concentrate plankton, and with it tuna, sharks and seabirds.

Polar open ocean.about: Cold, deep, seasonally ice-covered ocean. Short food chains built on krill and copepods support the largest animals that have ever lived.

Arctic.about: The ice-covered top of the world. A small, young fauna — the Arctic Ocean was largely frozen over until a few million years ago — but extraordinarily productive in the brief summer.

Temperate Northern Atlantic.about: From the Gulf of Maine to the Mediterranean. The most heavily fished sea on Earth, and the one whose stocks are the longest studied.

Temperate Northern Pacific.about: Cool, storm-driven coasts on both sides of the North Pacific, defined by the largest kelp forests anywhere.

Tropical Atlantic.about: The Caribbean, Brazilian and West African coasts. Far fewer coral species than the Indo-Pacific, but a high proportion found nowhere else.

Western Indo-Pacific.about: The Indian Ocean from East Africa to the Andaman Sea. Monsoon-driven, with coral reefs, seagrass meadows and the world's dugong stronghold.

Central Indo-Pacific.about: The Coral Triangle and its surroundings — the richest marine region on the planet, holding more coral and reef fish species than anywhere else.

Eastern Indo-Pacific.about: The scattered islands of the central Pacific. Isolation keeps species numbers low but endemism very high — a quarter of Hawaii's reef fish live nowhere else.

Tropical Eastern Pacific.about: From the Gulf of California to Ecuador, including the Galápagos. Cut off from the Atlantic three million years ago and from the central Pacific by open water.

Temperate South America.about: The Patagonian shelf, Chilean fjords and southern Brazil. Cold, productive, and a nursery for southern right whales and penguins.

Temperate Southern Africa.about: Where the warm Agulhas and cold Benguela meet around the Cape — one of the sharpest marine transitions in the world.

Temperate Australasia.about: Southern Australia and New Zealand. Long isolation produced a temperate reef fauna with the highest endemism of any such region.

Southern Ocean.about: The ring of water around Antarctica, sealed off by the Antarctic Circumpolar Current. Fish here carry antifreeze proteins in their blood.

Atlantic Warm Water.about: Open Atlantic beyond the shelf — gyres, the Gulf Stream, the Sargasso Sea and the equatorial band.

Indo-Pacific Warm Water.about: The vast warm open ocean of the Indian and Pacific basins, including the largest tuna fisheries on Earth.

Northern Cold Water.about: Subarctic open ocean. Enormous seasonal plankton blooms feed herring, capelin and the whales that follow them.

Southern Cold Water.about: Subantarctic and Antarctic open ocean, driven by krill — probably the most abundant animal by weight on the planet.

Western Coral Triangle.title: Western Coral Triangle
Western Coral Triangle.about: The single richest patch of ocean on Earth — over 500 reef-building coral species and more than 2,000 reef fish, centred on the Philippines, eastern Indonesia and Sabah.

Northeast Australian Shelf.title: Great Barrier Reef
Northeast Australian Shelf.about: The largest coral reef system in the world — 2,300 km of reef visible from orbit, and the most intensively monitored, after repeated mass bleaching since 2016.

Hawaii.title: Hawaiian Islands
Hawaii.about: The most isolated archipelago on Earth. A quarter of Hawaii's reef fish and a third of its invertebrates occur nowhere else.

Galapagos.title: Galápagos
Galapagos.about: Where cold Humboldt water meets the equator. Penguins and fur seals live alongside tropical corals — a collision of faunas found nowhere else.

Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.title: Red Sea
Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.about: Hot, very salty and almost closed off. Roughly 14% of its reef fish live nowhere else, and its corals tolerate temperatures that would bleach reefs elsewhere.

Mediterranean Sea.title: Mediterranean Sea
Mediterranean Sea.about: Nearly landlocked, warm and salty, and the most invaded sea on Earth — over a thousand non-native species have arrived, most through the Suez Canal.

Northern European Seas.title: North Sea, Baltic & Norwegian coast
Northern European Seas.about: Shallow, cool and fished for a thousand years. The Baltic is the world's largest body of brackish water, with a fauna squeezed between marine and freshwater.

Cold Temperate Northeast Pacific.title: Northeast Pacific kelp coast
Cold Temperate Northeast Pacific.about: From Alaska to Point Conception: the world's greatest kelp forests, and a textbook case of how sea otters keep urchins from eating them.

Tropical Northwestern Atlantic.title: Caribbean & Gulf of Mexico
Tropical Northwestern Atlantic.about: The Atlantic's coral heartland. Reef cover has fallen sharply since the 1980s, and lionfish from the Indo-Pacific are now established throughout.

Continental High Antarctic.title: Antarctic continental shelf
Continental High Antarctic.about: Water at −1.8 °C year-round under seasonal ice. Fish here survive on antifreeze glycoproteins, and giant invertebrates grow slowly for decades.

Benguela.title: Benguela upwelling
Benguela.about: Cold water dragged up along the Namibian and South African coast. One of the four great upwelling systems, and one of the most productive seas on the planet.

Agulhas.title: Agulhas coast
Agulhas.about: Where the warm Agulhas Current sweeps down South Africa's east coast, driving the sardine run — one of the largest animal migrations by sheer biomass.

Magellanic.title: Patagonian shelf & fjords
Magellanic.about: Cold, wind-hammered and hugely productive. The Patagonian shelf break is one of the busiest feeding fronts in the Southern Hemisphere.

Warm Temperate Southeastern Pacific.title: Humboldt coast
Warm Temperate Southeastern Pacific.about: The Peruvian and Chilean coast, fed by the strongest upwelling on Earth. A single fish — the anchoveta — has at times made up a tenth of the global catch.

Southern New Zealand.title: Southern New Zealand
Southern New Zealand.about: Cool subantarctic-influenced water around New Zealand's south. Long isolation makes it one of the most endemic temperate marine faunas anywhere.

Sunda Shelf.title: Sunda Shelf
Sunda Shelf.about: The shallow drowned continent between Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula — dry land during the ice ages, now warm reef and seagrass sea.

Gulf of Guinea.title: Gulf of Guinea
Gulf of Guinea.about: Warm, turbid and river-fed, with big seasonal upwelling. Nesting beaches here take a large share of the Atlantic's leatherback turtles.

Black Sea.title: Black Sea
Black Sea.about: Brackish at the surface and permanently anoxic below about 150 m — the largest body of oxygen-free water on Earth. Almost nothing lives in the deep.

Somali/Arabian.title: Arabian Sea & Somali coast
Somali/Arabian.about: Driven by the monsoon, which reverses the currents twice a year and triggers the only large upwelling in the Northern Indian Ocean.

Gulf Stream.title: Gulf Stream
Gulf Stream.about: A river in the ocean carrying more water than every river on land combined, dragging tropical animals north to the latitude of Newfoundland.

Kuroshio.title: Kuroshio Current
Kuroshio.about: The Pacific's western boundary current. Warm, deep blue and nutrient-poor, it carries tropical larvae as far north as Japan's Tohoku coast.

California Current.title: California Current
California Current.about: Cold water sliding south along western North America, upwelling as it goes. Productivity swings hard between El Niño and La Niña years.

North Central Atlantic Gyre.title: Sargasso Sea
North Central Atlantic Gyre.about: The only sea with no coastline, ringed by currents instead of land. Floating sargassum rafts make a drifting nursery in otherwise empty blue water.

Antarctic.title: Antarctic open ocean
Antarctic.about: South of the Polar Front, where krill turn a short summer of light into food for whales, seals and penguins across an entire ocean.

Indonesian Through-Flow.title: Indonesian Throughflow
Indonesian Through-Flow.about: The only tropical passage between two oceans, funnelling Pacific water into the Indian Ocean through a maze of straits and deep basins.

Equatorial Pacific.title: Equatorial Pacific
Equatorial Pacific.about: A band of upwelling stretching a third of the way around the planet, and the engine room of El Niño.
